concepts.name: Solutions and their defining traits
concepts.statement: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute particles are individually dispersed among the solvent’s, so its composition is uniform, its state is usually the solvent’s, and its solute never settles out. Almost any gas, liquid or solid can act as a solvent, so air and brass are solutions just as saltwater is.

concepts.name: Ideal solutions and matter dispersal
concepts.statement: When the attractions between unlike particles are no different from those between like particles, a solution forms with no change in energy, and it forms anyway, driven by the increased dispersal of matter alone.

concepts.name: Dissolution as three steps
concepts.statement: The formation of a solution may be viewed as separating the solute particles and the solvent particles, both endothermic, and then letting solute and solvent attract one another (solvation), which is exothermic. The balance of the three steps decides whether dissolving releases or absorbs heat.

concepts.name: Heat released or absorbed on dissolving
concepts.statement: A solute whose solvation releases more energy than its separation costs dissolves exothermically, as sodium hydroxide does; one whose separation costs more dissolves endothermically, as ammonium nitrate does, and it can still dissolve because of the increase in dispersal.

concepts.name: Predict whether two substances form a solution
concepts.statement: Naming the strongest attractions within the solute, within the solvent and between the two lets us predict whether they will mix and which solvent suits a solute.

concepts.name: Alloy
concepts.statement: An alloy is a solid mixture of a metallic element and one or more additional elements.

concepts.name: Spontaneous process
concepts.statement: A spontaneous process is a physical or chemical change that occurs without the addition of energy from an external source.

concepts.name: Solvation
concepts.statement: Solvation is the exothermic process in which intermolecular attractions between solute and solvent form as the solute particles are surrounded by solvent particles.

concepts.name: Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes
concepts.statement: An electrolyte yields ions when it dissolves, so its solution conducts electricity; a nonelectrolyte yields none. A strong electrolyte yields ions essentially completely, a weak electrolyte only in small part.

concepts.name: Ion-dipole attraction
concepts.statement: The electrostatic attraction between an ion and a polar molecule turns the negative oxygen ends of water molecules toward a cation and the positive hydrogen ends toward an anion, and it is what lets water pull ions out of a solid.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds dissociate
concepts.statement: When an ionic compound dissolves, water surrounds and solvates its ions and they disperse through the solution, a physical change called dissociation. Ionic compounds dissociate nearly completely, so even a sparingly soluble one is a strong electrolyte.

concepts.name: Covalent electrolytes react with water
concepts.statement: Some covalent compounds conduct once dissolved because their molecules react chemically with water to form ions: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely and is a strong electrolyte, while weak acids and bases ionize partly and are weak electrolytes.

concepts.name: Classify a solute as a strong, weak or nonelectrolyte
concepts.statement: Whether a solute is ionic, a strong acid, a weak acid or base, or an unreactive covalent compound tells us how well its solution will conduct.

concepts.name: Electrolyte
concepts.statement: An electrolyte is a substance that produces ions when dissolved in water, so that its solution conducts electricity.

concepts.name: Nonelectrolyte
concepts.statement: A nonelectrolyte is a substance that does not produce ions when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Strong electrolyte
concepts.statement: A strong electrolyte is a substance that dissociates or ionizes completely when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Weak electrolyte
concepts.statement: A weak electrolyte is a substance that ionizes only partially when dissolved in water.

concepts.name: Solubility, saturated and unsaturated solutions
concepts.statement: The solubility of a solute is the maximum concentration it can reach in a solvent under given conditions when dissolution is at equilibrium. A solution at that concentration is saturated, one below it is unsaturated.

concepts.name: Supersaturated solutions
concepts.statement: A solution can hold more solute than its solubility, a nonequilibrium state that ends in precipitation or loss of gas when it is disturbed. Cooling a saturated solution of a solid, or warming or depressurizing a solution of a gas, can prepare one.

concepts.name: Gases grow less soluble as temperature rises
concepts.statement: Since a gaseous solute has no solute-solute attraction to overcome, only its attraction to the solvent sets its solubility, and that solubility typically decreases as the temperature increases, which is why thermal pollution starves natural waters of oxygen.

concepts.name: Henry’s law
concepts.statement: The quantity of an ideal gas that dissolves in a definite volume of liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas, $C_{\text{g}} = kP_{\text{g}}$, with k set by the gas, the solvent and the temperature. A gas that reacts with the solvent, as ammonia does with water, dissolves more than the law predicts.

concepts.name: Calculate a gas solubility with Henry’s law
concepts.statement: Finding k from one known solubility and pressure gives the solubility at any other pressure, and a constant read from a solubility graph answers whether a stream holds enough oxygen for its fish.

concepts.name: Miscible, immiscible and partially miscible liquids
concepts.statement: Liquids of similar polarity mix in all proportions because the attractions between unlike molecules are as strong as those between like ones, an illustration of “like dissolves like”; a nonpolar liquid and water form separate layers, and some pairs are only partially miscible.

concepts.name: Solubility curves of solids
concepts.statement: The solubilities of most solids in water increase with temperature, though some, such as cerium sulfate, decrease, and a solubility curve reads off how much of a solid dissolves in 100 g of water at any temperature.

concepts.name: Saturated solution
concepts.statement: A saturated solution has a concentration equal to the solubility of its solute, the maximum concentration possible at that temperature and pressure.

concepts.name: Unsaturated solution
concepts.statement: An unsaturated solution has a concentration less than the solubility of its solute.

concepts.name: Miscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are miscible when they are mutually soluble in all proportions.

concepts.name: Immiscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are immiscible when their mutual solubility is negligible.

concepts.name: Partially miscible
concepts.statement: Liquids are partially miscible when they are of moderate mutual solubility.

concepts.name: Colligative properties
concepts.statement: Vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the total concentration of solute particles, not on their identity, mass or size.

concepts.name: Molality and mole fraction
concepts.statement: Because mole fraction and molality are built from masses and moles, either can be converted into the other, or into molarity or mass percentage, with the molar masses of the components and, for molarity, the density of the solution. Unlike molarity, neither changes with temperature.

concepts.name: Raoult’s law and vapor pressure lowering
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a component of an ideal solution is its mole fraction times the vapor pressure of the pure component, so a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent in proportion to how much it dilutes the solvent.

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.statement: The vapor above a mixture of two volatile liquids is richer in the more volatile one, so heating the mixture and condensing the vapor separates them; a fractionating column repeats the separation many times over.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation
concepts.statement: Because a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, the solution must be hotter than the pure solvent before its vapor pressure reaches the atmosphere’s, and the elevation is proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{b}} = K_{\text{b}}m$.

concepts.name: Freezing point depression
concepts.statement: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its pure solvent, by an amount proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{f}} = K_{\text{f}}m$, because only the solvent freezes out; salted roads and antifreeze exploit it.

concepts.name: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
concepts.statement: Solvent diffuses through a semipermeable membrane into a solution faster than it returns, until the solution’s rising pressure equalizes the rates; that pressure is the osmotic pressure, $\Pi = MRT$. Applying more pressure reverses osmosis, and a cell swells or shrivels in a hypotonic or hypertonic solution.

concepts.name: Determine a molar mass from a colligative property
concepts.statement: A measured freezing point depression, boiling point elevation or osmotic pressure gives the moles of solute in a known mass, and so the solute’s molar mass.

concepts.name: Colligative properties of electrolytes and the van’t Hoff factor
concepts.statement: An electrolyte yields more than one particle per formula unit, so its colligative effects are multiplied by the van’t Hoff factor i, the moles of particles per mole of formula units; residual attraction between ions, even ion pairs, makes the measured i smaller than predicted.

concepts.name: Molality, $m = \text{mol solute}/\text{kg solvent}$
concepts.statement: Molality is a concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute divided by the mass of the solvent in kilograms. Since it is built from moles and masses, it does not change with temperature.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation constant, $K_b$
concepts.statement: The boiling point elevation constant, or ebullioscopic constant, of a solvent is the proportionality constant relating the boiling point elevation of its solutions to the molality of solute.

concepts.name: Freezing point depression constant, $K_f$
concepts.statement: The freezing point depression constant, or cryoscopic constant, of a solvent is the proportionality constant relating the freezing point depression of its solutions to the molality of solute.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membrane
concepts.statement: A semipermeable membrane is a membrane that selectively permits the passage of certain ions or molecules.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.statement: Osmosis is the diffusion of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane.

concepts.name: Isotonic
concepts.statement: Two solutions are isotonic when they have equal osmotic pressures.

concepts.name: Hypertonic
concepts.statement: A solution is hypertonic to another when its osmotic pressure is greater.

concepts.name: Hypotonic
concepts.statement: A solution is hypotonic to another when its osmotic pressure is less.

concepts.name: Crenation
concepts.statement: Crenation is the shriveling of biological cells as they lose water by osmosis, as red blood cells do in a hypertonic solution.

concepts.name: Hemolysis
concepts.statement: Hemolysis is the rupture of red blood cells as they take up excess water by osmosis, as they do in a hypotonic solution.

concepts.name: Ion pair
concepts.statement: An ion pair is a solvated cation and anion held together by moderate electrostatic attraction, which lowers the number of independent particles in a solution of an electrolyte.

concepts.name: Colloids between solutions and suspensions
concepts.statement: A colloid’s particles are larger than most molecules yet small enough not to settle, so a colloid is intermediate between a solution, whose particles are molecules or ions, and a suspension, whose particles settle; colloidal particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase and dispersion medium
concepts.statement: A colloid’s minor, particulate component is the dispersed phase and the substance it is spread through is the dispersion medium, and nearly every combination of states occurs: sols, aerosols, emulsions, foams and gels.

concepts.name: Preparing colloids and emulsions
concepts.statement: Colloidal particles are made by dispersion, grinding larger particles down, or by condensation, growing them from molecules or ions; an emulsion of two immiscible liquids is kept from separating by an emulsifying agent.

concepts.name: How soaps and detergents clean
concepts.statement: Soap and detergent molecules are amphiphilic, a nonpolar hydrocarbon end and an ionic end, so they gather at the boundary between grease and water and suspend the grease as colloidal particles that wash away.

concepts.name: Colloidal particles are charged
concepts.statement: The particles of one colloid carry charges of the same sign, which keeps them dispersed by repulsion, and highly charged electrodes attract, neutralize and deposit them, as in the Cottrell precipitator that cleans smoke.

concepts.name: Colloid
concepts.statement: A colloid, or colloidal dispersion, is a mixture in which relatively large solid or liquid particles are dispersed uniformly throughout a gas, liquid or solid and do not settle.

concepts.name: Suspension
concepts.statement: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which relatively large particles are temporarily dispersed but settle out over time.

concepts.name: The Tyndall effect
concepts.statement: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of visible light by a colloidal dispersion, which makes the path of a beam visible through it.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase
concepts.statement: The dispersed phase of a colloid is the substance present as relatively large solid or liquid particles.

concepts.name: Dispersion medium
concepts.statement: The dispersion medium of a colloid is the solid, liquid or gas in which the colloidal particles are dispersed.

concepts.name: Emulsion
concepts.statement: An emulsion is a colloid formed from immiscible liquids.

concepts.name: Gel
concepts.statement: A gel is a colloidal dispersion of a liquid in a solid.

concepts.name: Amphiphilic
concepts.statement: A molecule is amphiphilic when it has both a hydrophobic, nonpolar part and a hydrophilic, polar part.

concepts.name: Emulsifying agent
concepts.statement: An emulsifying agent is an amphiphilic substance used to stabilize the particles of an emulsion.
